power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .105", "p = .703", "p = .783", "p = .644", "p = .310", "p = .568", "p = .635", "p = .612"), Sentence = c("The Interactive (R² = .38, p < .001) and Sensory (R² = .07, p = .002) subfactors explained significant variance, whereas the corresponding estimate for Investigative Curiosity (R² = .07, p = .105) did not reach significance.", "Scores for girls (M = 6.00) and boys (M = 5.98) did not differ significantly, t(285) = -0.38, p = .703.", "Mean scores were not significantly associated with caregiver education (rs = .016, p = .783) or child age (rs = -.03, p = .644).", "Mean scores were not significantly associated with caregiver education (rs = .016, p = .783) or child age (rs = -.03, p = .644).", "Investigative Curiosity was not significantly associated with age (rs = .06, p = .310).", "Interactive Curiosity was positively associated with Social Cognition (b = 1.51, SE = 0.40, t(55) = 3.81, p < .001), with age showing a positive association (b = 0.40, 370 SE = 0.12, t(55) = 3.23, p = .002), but sex did not (p = .568).", "Linear regressions confirmed that Sensory Curiosity was not significantly associated with Visual Sensation Seeking even after adjustment for age and sex (b = -0.09, SE = 0.19, t(55) = -0.48, p = .635; #### Careless Responding

54 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **12 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 2 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: The Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire: a German Validation and its Associations with Early Cognition

author.affiliation:
Georg-Elias-Müller-Institut für Psychologie
								University of Göttingen
								
									Göttingen
									Germany

Department of Psychology
								Lancaster University
								
									Lancaster
									United Kingdom

text.text: We thank all adults, families and children who participated in the studies.
We further thank Malte Spreckelsen, Annika Rohloff, and Maria Carmen Wiemann López for their help with data collection.
We thank Gert Westermann for helpful discussions and Nivedita Mani for participant compensation.

Curiosity in infancy is considered a key driver of learning, motivating infants' exploration of the environment and supporting their acquisition of language as well as their emerging understanding of objects and social interactions (Jirout et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Curiosity in infancy is considered a key driver of learning, motivating infants' exploration of the environment and supporting their acquisition of language as well as their emerging understanding of objects and social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Jirout et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Theoretical models have long highlighted its role in cognitive and 60 socioemotional development, yet empirical tools to quantify stable, trait-like individual differences in curiosity have been scarce for infants under two years (Kidd & Hayden, 2015).
text.formatted: Theoretical models have long highlighted its role in cognitive and 60 socioemotional development, yet empirical tools to quantify stable, trait-like individual differences in curiosity have been scarce for infants under two years <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Kidd & Hayden, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire (ITCQ) addressed this gap with a validated caregiver-report instrument for 5-to 24-month-olds in the UK (Altmann et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: The Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire (ITCQ) addressed this gap with a validated caregiver-report instrument for 5-to 24-month-olds in the UK <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Altmann et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we extend this tool to a German sample and 65 investigate its correlation with further cognitive abilities in early childhood.

Empirical research shows that even infants selectively attend to informative cues and engage in exploration that guides their learning (e.g., Begus et al., 2014; Begus & Southgate, 2012; Lucca & Wilbourn, 2018).
text.formatted: Empirical research shows that even infants selectively attend to informative cues and engage in exploration that guides their learning (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Begus et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Begus & Southgate, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Lucca & Wilbourn, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Experimental work has typically operationalised infant curiosity through laboratory tasks that index state curiosity, 70 such as selective attention to novel events or exploration of uncertain outcomes (e.g., Altmann et al., 2025b; Poli et al., 2024; Stahl & Feigenson, 2015).
text.formatted: Experimental work has typically operationalised infant curiosity through laboratory tasks that index state curiosity, 70 such as selective attention to novel events or exploration of uncertain outcomes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Altmann et al., 2025b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Poli et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stahl & Feigenson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, caregiver-report measures capture tendencies across everyday situations and provide a complementary approach to studying individual differences (Lee et al., 2023; Piotrowski et al., 2014). 75 The ITCQ focuses on observable exploration behaviours, with items capturing general tendencies to explore the immediate environment and request information.
text.formatted: In contrast, caregiver-report measures capture tendencies across everyday situations and provide a complementary approach to studying individual differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Lee et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Piotrowski et al., 2014)</ref>. <ref type="bibr">75</ref> The ITCQ focuses on observable exploration behaviours, with items capturing general tendencies to explore the immediate environment and request information.

text.text: In a large UK sample, exploratory factor analyses and structural equation modelling supported a 23-item scale with good internal consistency, an overall curiosity score, and three subscales: Sensory, Investigative, and Interactive Curiosity (Altmann et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: In a large UK sample, exploratory factor analyses and structural equation modelling supported a 23-item scale with good internal consistency, an overall curiosity score, and three subscales: Sensory, Investigative, and Interactive Curiosity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Altmann et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: These facets reflect broad sensory exploration, independent investigation, and the use of social partners as information sources.
The ITCQ also showed theoretically meaningful associations with temperament, supporting its validity as a trait measure.
Its extension, the Early Childhood Curiosity Questionnaire, assesses curiosity between two and five years across the UK, the Netherlands, and Germany 85 (Altmann & De Boer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Its extension, the Early Childhood Curiosity Questionnaire, assesses curiosity between two and five years across the UK, the Netherlands, and Germany 85 <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Altmann & De Boer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond temperament, early curiosity may be linked to children's emerging cognitive competencies.

Longitudinal research has related infant exploratory behaviour (Bornstein et al., 2013; Muentener et al., 2018) as well as an ad hoc measure of parent reported curiosity (Shah et al., 2018) to later cognitive and 90 academic outcomes.
text.formatted: Longitudinal research has related infant exploratory behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bornstein et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Muentener et al., 2018)</ref> as well as an ad hoc measure of parent reported curiosity <ref type="bibr">(Shah et al., 2018)</ref> to later cognitive and 90 academic outcomes.

text.text: However, these findings leave open how trait-like, everyday curiosity relates to specific aspects of cognition during infancy and toddlerhood.
Examining such associations can help situate the ITCQ within early development while providing additional evidence for its construct validity.
Three conceptually related constructs are particularly relevant.
Sensory 95 Curiosity may overlap with Visual Sensation Seeking, the tendency to seek visually stimulating input (Piccardi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Sensory 95 Curiosity may overlap with Visual Sensation Seeking, the tendency to seek visually stimulating input <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Piccardi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Investigative Curiosity may be associated with Independent Problem Solving, which involves working out solutions without help or demonstration (Hoicka et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Investigative Curiosity may be associated with Independent Problem Solving, which involves working out solutions without help or demonstration <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hoicka et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Interactive Curiosity may relate to Social Cognition, including joint attention and understanding others' behaviour (Hoicka et 100 al., 2022).
text.formatted: Interactive Curiosity may relate to Social Cognition, including joint attention and understanding others' behaviour <ref type="bibr">(Hoicka et 100 al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These conceptual links motivate examining positive associations between the corresponding measures, without assuming that the constructs are interchangeable or that the relations are exclusive to particular subscales.
properties generalise across linguistic and cultural settings.
As such, a Dutch and Italian adaptation have already provided evidence for its use in two other European samples (de Boer et al., 2026; Passaquindici et al., in revision).
text.formatted: As such, a Dutch and Italian adaptation have already provided evidence for its use in two other European samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(de Boer et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Passaquindici et al., in revision)</ref>.

text.text: The present manuscript reports two complementary studies to validate the ITCQ for the German population.
Study 1 evaluates the German ITCQ following the validation strategy of the original paper, focusing on its factor structure, reliability, and associations with 110 caregiver-reported temperament.
Study 2 examines associations with Visual Sensation Seeking, Independent Problem Solving, and Social Cognition in an independent sample.
Participants were recruited via the local child research database or through social media with the aim to collect at least 230 complete responses (about 10 per item, Altmann et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: Participants were recruited via the local child research database or through social media with the aim to collect at least 230 complete responses (about 10 per item, <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Altmann et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: The final sample included 291 responses about typically developing, German-speaking infants between 4.86 and 24.21 months (M = 14.26, SD = 5.10; 144 girls, 143 boys, four other/not reported).

Thirty-three additional 120 responses were excluded because they were incomplete (n = 13), contained only "not applicable" responses (n = 1), were about non-German children (n = 2), children outside the predefined age range (n = 9), or concerned children born prematurely (n = 6) or with reported developmental concerns (n = 2).
The majority of caregivers reported their child to be a firstborn (66%), with 125 25% second-born and 7% third or later-born.
The sample was predominantly monolingual (approximately 98%), and 79% of caregivers held a university degree (Bachelor's or higher).
Participants received a €6 bookstore voucher.
Ethics approval was granted by the local university ethics committee.
We measured infants' trait curiosity with the German ITCQ.

As data collection began before publication of the original UK questionnaire, we translated and distributed the full set of 34 original items: the 23 final items and 11 items subsequently excluded during the UK analysis.

These items describe typical exploration behaviours of young children (e.g., S8: "My child enthusiastically 135 explores new environments (e.g., a new house, the beach, etc.)") with German versions being developed via forward-backward translation (e.h., S8German: "Mein Kind erkundet mit Begeisterung neue Umgebungen (z.
B. ein neues Haus, den Strand usw.)").
Access to the German items is provided through the Open Science Framework (REDACTED LINK).
140 Caregivers rated each item on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 ("stimme überhaupt nicht zu", "do not agree at all") to 7 ("stimme voll und ganz zu", "strongly agree").
If caregivers could not recall a situation in which a behaviour could be observed, or the child was not yet able to show it, they were asked to choose "not applicable".
Scores were calculated as the means of the corresponding items, 145 excluding "not applicable" responses.
Two further items assessed concurrent validity.
The direct item ("Ich würde mein Kind als neugierig beschreiben", "I would describe my child as curious") used the same response scale.

The comparative item ("Im Vergleich zu anderen Kindern desselben Alters könnte mein Kind beschrieben werden als…", "Compared to other 150 children of the same age, I would describe my child as…") was rated from 1 ("weniger neugierig", "less curious") to 5 ("viel neugieriger", "much more curious").
Behavior Questionnaire for infants up to 12 months and the Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire for toddlers between 13 and 24 months (Putnam et al., 155 2006 (Putnam et al., 155 , 2014)).
text.formatted: Behavior Questionnaire for infants up to 12 months and the Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire for toddlers between 13 and 24 months <ref type="bibr">(Putnam et al., 155 2006</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Putnam et al., 155 , 2014))</ref>.

text.text: These questionnaires capture Surgency, Negative Affect, and Self-Regulation through caregiver ratings of the frequency of everyday behaviours.
They served as external validation criteria for assessing whether the German ITCQ showed similar associations with temperament to the original English measure.
Sociodemographic questions concerned the child's age and sex, birth order, 160 prematurity, developmental concerns, and caregiver education.

Data collection was conducted from November 2022 to the end of March 2023 using Qualtrics and from December 2023 to the end of January 2024 using LimeSurvey after an institutional change in data management policy.
Completion 165 took approximately 15-20 minutes.
After providing consent, caregivers completed the ITCQ with items in randomised order, the age-group-specific temperament questionnaire, and the demographic questions.
At the end, caregivers could provide their email address to receive a voucher and consent to being contacted for a retest one week later.
At retest, they completed 170 only the ITCQ and received no further compensation.
At both timepoints, participants were informed that participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw without negative consequences.
Analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2024) using psych (Revelle, 175 2024), lavaan (Rosseel, 2012), and irr (Gamer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2024) using psych <ref type="bibr">(Revelle, 175 2024)</ref>, lavaan <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Rosseel, 2012)</ref>, and irr <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Gamer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Only the final 23 ITCQ items were analysed.

Due to a technical error affecting the first 84 responses, Item retained where valid data were available but excluded from the test-retest analyses which were concentrated on this initial response pool.
Its behaviour in the remaining 180 majority of the final sample was directly checked and considered in line with expectations.

Before structural analyses, factorability of the 23-item correlation matrix was assessed using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy, the matrix determinant, and the mean inter-item correlation (Kaiser, 1974; Piedmont, 185 2014).
text.formatted: Before structural analyses, factorability of the 23-item correlation matrix was assessed using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy, the matrix determinant, and the mean inter-item correlation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kaiser, 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Piedmont, 185 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Structural validity was evaluated by testing the original factor structure (Altmann et al., 2025a) using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA).
text.formatted: Structural validity was evaluated by testing the original factor structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Altmann et al., 2025a)</ref> using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA).

text.text: A unidimensional model served as the baseline and a correlated three-factor model, comprising Sensory, Investigative, and Interactive Curiosity, as the target structure.
Both were estimated using maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR) for skewed 190 response distributions and full-information maximum likelihood (FIML) for missing data.

Model fit was evaluated using the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), and Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR; Hu & Bentler, 1999).
text.formatted: Model fit was evaluated using the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), and Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Hu & Bentler, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: The working criteria were 195 CFI and TLI ≥ .90, RMSEA ≤ .06, and SRMR ≤ .08.
Where initial fit was inadequate, modification indices were inspected and up to five residual covariances were freed iteratively.
Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's α, Guttman's lambda 6, and omega total for the full scale and each subscale.

Test-retest reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients from a two-way random-200 effects, absolute-agreement model for single measures, ICC(A,1), calculated for pooled item-occasion pairs and participant-level mean scores (Koo & Li, 2016).
text.formatted: Test-retest reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients from a two-way random-200 effects, absolute-agreement model for single measures, ICC(A,1), calculated for pooled item-occasion pairs and participant-level mean scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Koo & Li, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Exploratory analyses examined sex differences in mean curiosity scores and associations with age and caregiver education.
Spearman's rank-order correlations were used for age-related analyses because age and mean scores deviated from 205 normality.
Concurrent validity was assessed by correlating ITCQ mean scores with the two single-item caregiver ratings, also using Spearman's rho.
Associations with Surgency, Negative Affect, and Effortful Control were examined for the overall ITCQ score and each subscale.
Temperament dimension scores from the two age-specific questionnaires were pooled as indicators of the same broad constructs (Putnam et 210 al., 2008).
text.formatted: Temperament dimension scores from the two age-specific questionnaires were pooled as indicators of the same broad constructs <ref type="bibr">(Putnam et 210 al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: All tests were two-tailed, with α = .05.
ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Grammarly were used for text editing when writing the manuscript.
The KMO measure of sampling adequacy was .87, with all individual item measures ≥ .69.
The matrix determinant was positive and non-zero (1.77 × 10⁻⁵), and the mean inter-item correlation was r = .21.
These results supported proceeding with the factor analysis.

The correlated three-factor model with five freed residual covariances (Iv1-Iv3, Ia1-Ia2, S2-S5, S5-Iv1, and S3-Ia3) showed overall acceptable fit to the German data: CFI = .90, TLI = .89, RMSEA = .045, 90% CI [.036, .053], and SRMR = .067.
It represented a substantial improvement over the modified unidimensional model (CFI = .82, TLI = .79, RMSEA = .058, 90% CI [.051, .065], SRMR = .08; Δχ 2 (3) = 80.16, p < .001).
text.formatted: It represented a substantial improvement over the modified unidimensional model (CFI = .82, TLI = .79, RMSEA = .058, 90% CI [.051, .065], SRMR = .08; Δχ 2 (3) = 80.16, p < .001).

text.text: The Interactive (R² = .38, p < .001) and Sensory (R² = .07, p = .002) subfactors explained significant variance, whereas the corresponding estimate for Investigative Curiosity (R² = .07, p = .105) did not reach significance.
text.formatted: The Interactive (R² = .38, p < .001) and Sensory (R² = .07, p = .002) subfactors explained significant variance, whereas the corresponding estimate for Investigative Curiosity (R² = .07, p = .105) did not reach significance.

text.text: Factor 230 correlations were r = .88 between Sensory and Investigative, r = .90 between Investigative and Interactive, and r = .52 between Sensory and Interactive Curiosity.
The full 23-item scale showed good internal consistency (α = .85, λ6 = .88, ωT = .88).
Sensory and Interactive Curiosity showed acceptable-to-good consistency 235 (Sensory: α = .80, λ6 = .80, ωT = .83; Interactive: α = .74, λ6 = .74, ωT = .83).
Investigative Curiosity showed lower consistency (α = .56, λ6 = .53, ωT = .65).
Omega hierarchical for the full scale was ωH = .45 and Revelle's coefficient beta was β = .61 indicating a shared underlying latent curiosity factor.
Mean curiosity scores were generally high (M = 6.00 on a 1-7 scale), with limited variance (SDs approximately .49 for both boys and girls).
Scores for girls (M = 6.00) and boys (M = 5.98) did not differ significantly, t(285) = -0.38, p = .703.
Mean scores were not significantly associated with caregiver education (rs = .016, p = .783) or child age (rs = -.03, p = .644).
At the subscale level, Sensory Curiosity declined 245 with age (rs = -.21, p < .001), whereas Interactive Curiosity increased (rs = .21, p < .001).
text.formatted: At the subscale level, Sensory Curiosity declined 245 with age (rs = -.21, p < .001), whereas Interactive Curiosity increased (rs = .21, p < .001).

text.text: Investigative Curiosity was not significantly associated with age (rs = .06, p = .310).
Children below 12 months accounted for approximately 80% of the missing responses in line with the original questionnaire's response patterns.

The direct caregiver rating of curiosity was positively associated with mean 250 ITCQ scores (rs = .43, p < .001), as was the comparative rating relative to peers (rs = .21, p < .001), providing initial support for concurrent validity.
text.formatted: The direct caregiver rating of curiosity was positively associated with mean 250 ITCQ scores (rs = .43, p < .001), as was the comparative rating relative to peers (rs = .21, p < .001), providing initial support for concurrent validity.

text.text: A subsample of 65 caregivers completed the retest (Mage = 15.18 months, SD = 5.16, range = 5.75-23.46 months; 35 boys, 30 girls).
The interval ranged from 7 to 255 14 days (M = 8.02, SD = 1.49).
Seven responses completed after more than two weeks were excluded.
At the pooled item level, ICC(A,1) was .67, 95% CI [.64, .70], for the overall scale, .59 [.53, .63] for Sensory, .62 [.55, .69] for Investigative, and .67 [.61, .73] for Interactive Curiosity.
At the participant mean-score level, reliability was .85 [.77, .91] for the full scale, .85 [.77, .91] for Sensory, .57 [.38, .72] for 260 Investigative, and .75 [.62, .84] for Interactive Curiosity.
Overall Curiosity, Sensory Curiosity, and Investigative Curiosity were positively associated with Surgency, whereas Interactive Curiosity showed a small negative association (Table 1).
text.formatted: Overall Curiosity, Sensory Curiosity, and Investigative Curiosity were positively associated with Surgency, whereas Interactive Curiosity showed a small negative association (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Negative Affect was largely unrelated to curiosity 265 ratings but showed a small negative association with Interactive Curiosity.
Effortful Control was positively associated with the overall, Sensory, and Interactive scores, whereas its association with Investigative Curiosity was not significant.
Study 2 extended the validity evidence beyond temperament by examining associations with Visual Sensation Seeking, Independent Problem Solving, and Social Cognition in an independent sample.
Caregivers were recruited between February and April 2026 through social media.
Of 226 initiated questionnaires, 161 were incomplete (most already terminated before or at the Consent form), leaving 65 complete questionnaires.
Six 280 further responses were excluded because the child was older than 25 months (n = 2), was born before 37 weeks of gestation (n = 2), or had a reported diagnosed developmental concern (n = 2).
The final sample comprised 59 children (Mage = 14.04 months, SD = 3.43, range = 10.25-24.72 months; 40 boys, 19 girls), all but one completed by their mothers.
Children were reportedly mostly monolingual German-speaking (67.79%) or grew up exposed to German and at least one other language (32.21%).

Caregiver education comprised lower secondary education (n = 11), upper secondary education (n = 2), vocational or practical qualifications (n = 25), university education (n = 11), and advanced postgraduate education (n = 10), thereby being more 290 educationally diverse than the validation sample from Study 1.
Caregivers received a printable children's story as a non-monetary appreciation of their participation.
The local university ethics committee approved the study, and caregivers provided informed consent.
Caregivers completed the 23-item German ITCQ using the response format described in Study 1.
Visual Sensation Seeking was assessed using four items drawn from the Infant-Toddler Sensory Profile (Dunn & Daniels, 2002; Piccardi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Visual Sensation Seeking was assessed using four items drawn from the Infant-Toddler Sensory Profile <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Dunn & Daniels, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Piccardi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These items concern children's interest in moving or rotating objects, shiny objects, their own reflection, and rapidly changing colourful television content.
Responses ranged from 1 ("almost always") to 5 ("almost never") and were reversecoded so that higher scores indicated more Visual Sensation Seeking.
Independent Problem Solving was assessed using the 10-item Early Independent Problem Solving Survey (EIPSS; Hoicka et al., 2023), developed for children aged 12-47 months.
text.formatted: Independent Problem Solving was assessed using the 10-item Early Independent Problem Solving Survey (EIPSS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Hoicka et al., 2023)</ref>, developed for children aged 12-47 months.

text.text: Items concerned solving problems without assistance, 305 including building, puzzles, and working out how objects function.
Responses ranged from 1 ("strongly disagree") to 4 ("strongly agree"), with a "not applicable" option.
The overall mean score was used.
Social Cognition was assessed using the 21-item Early Social Cognition Inventory (ESCI; Hoicka et al., 2022), developed for children from birth to 47 months.
text.formatted: Social Cognition was assessed using the 21-item Early Social Cognition Inventory (ESCI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Hoicka et al., 2022)</ref>, developed for children from birth to 47 months.

text.text: 310 Items concerned social-cognitive behaviours, such as following another person's pointing gesture.
Responses were coded yes/no, and the number of "yes" responses was summed, yielding scores from 0 to 21.
No "not applicable" option was provided.
Negatively keyed ITCQ and EIPSS items were reverse-coded.
For the ITCQ, Visual Sensation Seeking, and Independent Problem Solving, available-item means 315 were calculated after excluding missing or "not applicable" responses.
The online questionnaire was administered using LimeSurvey and took approximately 15-20 minutes.
After consent and initial demographic questions, caregivers completed the ITCQ, Visual Sensation Seeking items, EIPSS, and ESCI 320 in that order.
Additional questions concerned parenting style, time spent together in everyday activities, and demographic characteristics; these additional measures were not analysed here.
Analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2026).
Internal consistency 325 was assessed using Cronbach's α for the Likert-format measures and KR-20 for the dichotomous ESCI items.
Pearson correlations described associations among the three ITCQ subscales and the three external measures.

Three separate multiple linear regressions examined the theory-motivated pairs: Visual Sensation Seeking with Sensory Curiosity, Independent Problem Solving with Investigative Curiosity, 330 and Social Cognition with Interactive Curiosity.
Each model included child age in months and sex as covariates, accounting for age-related differences and possible differences associated with sex.
The models estimate adjusted concurrent associations, not developmental or causal effects.
All tests were two-tailed with α = .05.
Reported p-values are unadjusted for multiple testing; findings are therefore 335 interpreted cautiously as initial validity evidence.
Internal consistency was good for Sensory (α = .80) and Interactive Curiosity (α = .84), but lower for Investigative Curiosity (α = .55), replicating result patterns 340 from Study 1.
Reliability was α = .61 for Visual Sensation Seeking, α = .71 for Independent Problem Solving, and KR-20 = .81 for Social Cognition.
Descriptive statistics are shown in Table 2, and the complete correlation matrix in Table 3.

text.text: The ITCQ subscales were moderately to strongly correlated to the tested cognitive constructs.
Independent Problem Solving was positively associated with 345 Sensory (r = .27, p < .05), Investigative (r = .32, p = .013), and Interactive Curiosity (r = .33, p < .05).

text.text: Social Cognition was positively associated with Interactive Curiosity (r = .52, p < .001), but its correlations with Sensory and Investigative Curiosity were not significant.

text.text: Visual Sensation Seeking was not significantly associated with any curiosity subscale but showed a small positive association with Social Cognition (r = 350 .27, p < .05).

text.text: Investigative Curiosity was positively associated with Independent Problem 365 Solving (b = 0.22, SE = 0.09, t(55) = 2.38, p = .021), whereas neither age nor sex was a significant predictor.
The overall model was significant, F(3, 55) = 3.32, p = .026, R² = .153.

Interactive Curiosity was positively associated with Social Cognition (b = 1.51, SE = 0.40, t(55) = 3.81, p < .001), with age showing a positive association (b = 0.40, 370 SE = 0.12, t(55) = 3.23, p = .002), but sex did not (p = .568).

text.text: Residuals in this model deviated slightly from normality (Shapiro-Wilk W = .95, p = .026), but Q-Q plots did not indicate pronounced departures.
The present studies evaluated the German Infant and Toddler Curiosity Questionnaire and examined its associations with aspects of early cognition.
Study 1 broadly replicated the original validation, with an overall acceptable three-factor solution, good internal consistency for the full scale, and short-term stability of caregiver ratings.

Study 2 extended the validity evidence and showed its relation 380 aspects of cognition: While Independent Problem Solving correlated positively with curiosity, Social Cognition showed the strongest correlation with Interactive Curiosity.
Visual Sensation Seeking did not correlate with curiosity.
Together, these findings validate and extend the original measure of young children's curiosity.
The Sensory and Interactive subscales showed acceptable-to-good internal 385 consistency, whereas Investigative Curiosity was less reliable in both studies.
We retained the original item structure to facilitate comparison with other language versions rather than refining the German scale within these samples.
The findings support its use for further research, while indicating that Investigative scores require particular care.

In fact, a recent independent cultural validation study (REDACTED) 390 has revealed that German parents rated some of the Investigative items as expressions of curiosity but also as less desirable behaviours for their children to present.
This could suggest one potential reason for the less robustly fitting subscale in the here reported samples, but more evidence would be needed to allow more founded conclusions.
As children got older, caregivers reported less Sensory and more Interactive Curiosity.

While in the original sample, Sensory Curiosity was unrelated to age (Altmann et al., 2025a), the Interactive results pattern is consistent with those initial findings as well as the increasing orientation towards social interactions during infancy (Thiele et al., 2021).
text.formatted: While in the original sample, Sensory Curiosity was unrelated to age <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Altmann et al., 2025a)</ref>, the Interactive results pattern is consistent with those initial findings as well as the increasing orientation towards social interactions during infancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Thiele et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Temperament associations were broadly similar to 400 those previously reported.
One exception was the small negative association between Surgency and Interactive Curiosity, contrasting with the positive association in the Dutch sample (de Boer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: One exception was the small negative association between Surgency and Interactive Curiosity, contrasting with the positive association in the Dutch sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(de Boer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such differences may reflect variation in samples, reporting, or opportunities for social exploration rather than a single cultural explanation.
405 Study 2 indicated that the German version of the ITCQ correlated with different measures of early cognition: Independent Problem Solving correlated positively with all three curiosity subscales.
Social Cognition was more selectively associated and showed the strongest overall correlation with Interactive Curiosity.

While the former association pattern corresponds to previous links between various forms of infant 410 exploration and later cognition (Bornstein et al., 2013; Muentener et al., 2018), the latter finding may indicate that Social Cognition is concretely important for social information seeking contexts but not in other forms of curious exploration.
text.formatted: While the former association pattern corresponds to previous links between various forms of infant 410 exploration and later cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bornstein et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Muentener et al., 2018)</ref>, the latter finding may indicate that Social Cognition is concretely important for social information seeking contexts but not in other forms of curious exploration.

text.text: Visual Sensation Seeking was not significantly associated with the ITCQ subscales.

This may reflect differences between enjoying perceptually stimulating input and broader 415 exploratory behaviour, but its low internal consistency and frequent "not applicable" responses limit interpretation.
Because Study 2 is cross-sectional, its findings are interpreted as concurrent associations rather than evidence for the direction of these relationships.
Together, these results motivate further work on how everyday information seeking and emerging cognitive skills are related.
420 Several further limitations warrant consideration.
Both studies relied on caregiver reports, and overlapping item content and shared reporting tendencies may contribute to associations.

In Study 1, the highly educated, predominantly monolingual sample limits generalisability, whereas age-related missingness, the S9 presentation error, and missing responses on the external measures also warrant 425 consideration when interpreting scores.
Furthermore, Study 2's cross-sectional design cannot establish whether curiosity precedes cognitive competencies, follows them, or develops reciprocally.

Taken together, the findings provide robust support for the German version of the ITCQ as a reliable and valid instrument for assessing early trait curiosity, while 430 also offering novel insights into its cognitive correlates.
The replication of the threefactor structure, alongside acceptable internal consistency and short-term stability, underscores the questionnaire's cross-cultural utility.
However, the comparatively weaker psychometric performance of the Investigative Curiosity subscale highlights a need for further refinement and validation in diverse samples.

The positive 435 associations with Independent Problem Solving and Interactive Curiosity suggest meaningful links between early curiosity and cognitive development, yet the differential patterns across subscales call for deeper investigation.
Future research should employ longitudinal designs and multi-method approaches to clarify the directionality and developmental dynamics of these relationships.
Ultimately, this 440 work lays a valuable foundation for cross-cultural studies on the role of curiosity in early learning and cognition.
